name: EM-LLM

paper.title: Human-inspired Episodic Memory for Infinite Context LLMs

construction.unit: event: the per-layer KV cache of 8-128 consecutive tokens plus one representative key
construction.kept_as: the model's own key-value pairs for the tokens; nothing is rewritten
construction.processing: a token whose surprise (-log p) exceeds mean + γ·std of the preceding 4,096 tokens opens a new event; optional refinement moves each boundary to maximise modularity (or minimise conductance) of the key-similarity graph
construction.writer: fixed rule over the base LLM's own token probabilities and attention keys (no extra model)

organization.structure: flat, time-ordered list of events, one store per layer
organization.stores: 128 initial tokens and a 4,096-token local window stay in context; events live in a KV store offloaded to CPU memory or disk, with representative keys kept for search
organization.index: one representative key per event and layer: mean of the keys of the 4 tokens with the highest accumulated attention

management.operations: append only; least-recently-used events are offloaded between GPU, CPU and disk

retrieval.query: mean attention query of the current 512-token chunk, per layer
retrieval.candidates: every event, ranked by dot product between the query and its representative key
retrieval.selection: take events in rank order until the token budget is filled (similarity buffer); +C variants reserve 30% for the ±1 neighbours of retrieved events, kept in a queue (contiguity buffer)

use.context: each layer attends to 128 initial tokens + its retrieved events (original order, one fixed position) + the local window
use.reasoning: ordinary decoding; retrieval is repeated for every 512-token chunk and every layer

classify.note: Events are a flat, time-ordered list; the contiguity buffer only adds temporal neighbours of what similarity already picked.

stages.ingestion: The input is fed in 512-token chunks; the first 128 tokens and the latest 4,096 tokens (1,024 for Phi) always stay in context, and older tokens become memory.
stages.construction: Tokens whose surprise exceeds a moving threshold (mean + γ·std over the preceding window) start a new event; events are clipped to 8-128 tokens, and an optional refinement shifts each boundary to improve modularity or conductance of the key-similarity graph.
stages.organization: Each layer keeps the events' key-value cache plus one representative key per event (mean of the 4 most-attended keys); boundaries are shared by all layers.
stages.update: Events are only appended; the KV cache is moved between GPU, CPU and disk by least-recent use.
stages.retrieval: For each chunk and layer, the mean query is compared by dot product with every representative key, and top events fill the token budget; +C variants also enqueue the neighbouring event on each side of retrieved ones (contiguity buffer, 30% of the budget).
stages.answer: The layer's softmax attention runs over initial tokens, retrieved events in original order at one fixed position, and the local window.

summary: Training-free KV-cache memory that cuts the token stream into events at points of high LLM surprise (optionally refined by graph modularity) and retrieves whole events per layer by similarity plus their temporal neighbours.
notes:
Long-context architecture, not an agent memory: memory is the base LLM's own KV cache grouped into events; evaluated on LongBench, ∞-Bench and extended passkey retrieval, extending InfLLM (fixed-size blocks) with surprise-based event boundaries.
VENUE: ICLR 2025 main conference (poster; OpenReview BI2int5SAC, listed in the ICLR 2025 proceedings); the arXiv v3 PDF carries the ICLR 2025 header.
DESIGN: §3.1-3.4, App. C, D.1, E.2-E.3; code em_llm/attention at commit edb2e4a.

sources.code_note: Latest commit (2025-03-06); code files unchanged since the 2024-10-11 initial release, which the README calls 'a version of the code' for the ICLR 2025 paper. The shipped configs enable neither refinement nor the contiguity buffer (the S variant), and give γ = 1 for every model.

abstract.text: EM-LLM gives a pretrained LLM an episodic memory without any fine-tuning. It splits the past token stream into events where the model is most surprised by the next token, can refine those boundaries with graph-clustering scores on attention keys, and at every step retrieves whole events per layer by similarity together with their temporal neighbours. On LongBench and ∞-Bench it improves on InfLLM across five base models, beats RAG and, on most tasks, full-context attention, and retrieves a passkey from 10M tokens. Its event boundaries also align with those that people report in podcast transcripts.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Memory is the model's own KV cache: nothing is summarised or rewritten, only grouped into events and fetched back.
Event boundaries come from the LLM's surprise; retrieval is per layer and per 512-token chunk, not once per question.
The released configs run the surprise-only variant; refinement and the contiguity buffer are flags.

open_questions: Table 1 reports, per base model, whichever variant scored best overall, so the headline gain over InfLLM includes a choice among four variants.
The comparison with RAG uses LLaMA-3.1-8B with a 4K+4K window while RAG gets 5 chunks of 300 words; token budgets are not matched.

text: The LLM's own surprise marks where one event ends: tokens above a moving threshold start a new event, and refinement can shift the cut to make events more internally similar.
Each event keeps its tokens' key-value cache and one representative key; the first 128 and the latest 4,096 tokens always stay in context.

text: For every 512-token chunk, each layer compares its mean query with all representative keys and takes the best events until its token budget is full; +C variants also add each retrieved event's neighbours.
Attention then runs over the initial tokens, the retrieved events in their original order and the local window.

discussion.takeaway: Grouping a frozen LLM's KV cache into surprise-defined events and fetching whole events per layer is a cheap, training-free way to extend context. It beats fixed-size blocks (InfLLM) on most tasks and, with LLaMA-3.1-8B, beats both RAG and full-context attention on LongBench.

claims.claim: EM-LLM improves on InfLLM across base models.
claims.evidence: LongBench avg 43.7 vs 41.9 (Mistral), 51.3 vs 51.1 (LLaMA-3.1), 35.4 vs 34.5 (Phi-3); significant at benchmark level except Phi-3.5 (p = 0.23). Table 1, App. A.1

claims.claim: It beats RAG and full context.
claims.evidence: LLaMA-3.1-8B LongBench 51.58 vs 39.30 full context and 36.44 RAG (NV-Embed-v2); ∞-Bench 66.66 vs 66.33 and 58.97. Table 9, Fig. 1
100% on extended Passkey.Retrieval up to 10.2M tokens. §4.1, Fig. 1

claims.claim: Surprise-based events match human event boundaries and group similar keys.
claims.evidence: Surprise methods are closest to human podcast annotations (Fig. 4B) and score higher modularity and intra/inter similarity than fixed blocks on PG-19 (Table 2).
Refinement is best in 60% of tasks, the contiguity buffer in 44%. §4.4, Tables 3-7

limits: Memory is non-parametric storage of key-value pairs, unlike synaptic change in the brain.
Text only in the current implementation; no multi-modal episodes.
No consolidation of memories over time.
The authors claim an episodic-memory-inspired method, not evidence that the model uses it like human episodic memory.
reading: Gains over InfLLM are small on LongBench for LLaMA-3 and LLaMA-3.1 (+0.2 each in Table 1), and for LLaMA-3 the ∞-Bench average is lower than InfLLM's (48.81-49.00 vs 50.31 across variants, Table 4).
Table 1 shows a different best variant per model, and no variant wins everywhere (Tables 3-7), so which component helps depends on model and task.

Full context scores 100 on PassageRetrieval and leads on several QA tasks, but gets 4.5 on TREC, 8.68 on SAMSum, 19.30 on LCC and 18.33 on RepoBench-P (Table 9); the 12-point LongBench average gap comes mostly from these few tasks.
In the released code the refinement graph is one matrix summed over layers ≥ 20 and all heads, and the same boundaries serve every layer, while the paper describes per-head key similarity.
Retrieval is per layer and per 512-token chunk, so it is not comparable to question-time retrieval in agent memory systems.
